For the full brain install > — CLI, engine, skills, dream cycle — follow > [INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md](../../INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md); the README covers the > bootstrap and connect paths. Connect with [Option 2](#option-2-openclaw-mcp-add) (stdio) when the brain runs on the gateway's machine, or with [OpenClaw's own MCP client](#remote-brain-openclaws-mcp-client-over-https) when it runs elsewhere. Option 1's ClawHub bundle is not available yet. A bot that several people DM connects over HTTP as well: see [One bot for several people, in DMs](#one-bot-for-several-people-in-dms). ## Option 1: ClawHub bundle plugin (not available yet) This project publishes no ClawHub package yet. The package named `gbrain` on ClawHub is an unofficial upload of an old 0.10.1 build whose manifest has no `id`, so `openclaw plugins install clawhub:gbrain` stops with `plugin manifest requires id`. Don't install it; use Option 2. GBrain ships [`openclaw.plugin.json`](../../openclaw.plugin.json) at the repo root. Installing the bundle plugin registers the MCP server for you — the manifest carries an `mcpServers.gbrain` entry that runs the bundled `.agents/gbrain-launcher serve` (the same launcher the Codex and Claude Code plugins use; it resolves your installed `gbrain` via `GBRAIN_BIN`, then `~/.bun/bin/gbrain`, then `PATH`, so it works under launchd's bare PATH and never needs a build step) plus the bundled skills — and declares the `gbrain-context-engine` context engine. To route OpenClaw's context-engine slot through gbrain, two steps, in this order: 1. Install and enable the plugin by its own id, `gbrain-context-engine` (the `id` in `openclaw.plugin.json`). 2. Set the slot to the engine id the plugin registers: ``` plugins.slots.contextEngine = gbrain-context-engine ``` The current host requires the canonical plugin ID in the slot. The installed plugin ID is unchanged and `gbrain-context` remains a registry alias for older integrations, but it is not a slot alias on current hosts: migrate an old `plugins.slots.contextEngine = gbrain-context` setting to `gbrain-context-engine`. Setting the slot alone does not install/enable the plugin. For a legacy host that cannot provide a per-session workspace, set `plugins.entries.gbrain-context-engine.config.workspaceDir` to an absolute workspace path; on multi-agent hosts prefer the host-supplied workspace. An unbound or ambiguous workspace warns and reads no source rather than selecting an arbitrary agent's memory. The factory also accepts zero arguments from current hosts. Its `assemble` keeps the current prompt separate from fenced stored transcript history; an identical trailing legacy user message is already the current turn. The admitted-turn acknowledgement is stateless and writes nothing. Reflex-only pointer synthesis leaves returned messages unchanged; the turn acknowledgement does not automatically capture conversation content (compaction has its own explicit checkpoint path). Loading the plugin alone is not evidence of model recall: verify saved-page retrieval after a restarted turn and source isolation with the intended host. The loopback native test uses a deterministic provider, so it does not certify paid-model recall or provenance. ## Option 2: `openclaw mcp add` OpenClaw keeps MCP servers under `mcp.servers` in `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` (`openclaw config schema` shows the key path). Register gbrain with the CLI: ```bash openclaw mcp add gbrain --command "$(command -v gbrain)" --arg serve --arg --surface --arg starter --arg --advertise --arg verbs --env GBRAIN_HOME=$HOME ``` Use an absolute `--command` path: the launchd-started gateway's `PATH` does not include `~/.bun/bin`, so a bare `gbrain` fails to spawn. `--env` is optional: a PGLite brain needs no `DATABASE_URL` (`--env DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...` for Postgres), and `GBRAIN_HOME` only matters when the brain home isn't `~/.gbrain`. `--surface starter --advertise verbs` lists the seven-verb memory protocol ([MEMORY_VERBS v1](../protocol/MEMORY_VERBS_v1.md)) plus `request_tools`, which reaches every other tool; drop the `--advertise verbs` values to list the starter set (`full` for the whole catalog) (check `openclaw mcp add --help` for your version's `--arg` spelling). Leave `GBRAIN_SOURCE` unset in the MCP env unless you deliberately want single-source retrieval: a pin scopes every tool (search, `get_brain_identity` counts, …) to that one source, and nothing warns on reads. ## Remote brain: OpenClaw's MCP client over HTTPS When the brain runs on another machine, OpenClaw connects to its MCP endpoint itself, over streamable HTTP with OAuth. That grant is scoped and revocable on the brain host, while the stdio route above gives the gateway full local database access. ```bash openclaw gateway stop openclaw mcp add gbrain --url https:///mcp --transport streamable-http --auth oauth openclaw mcp login gbrain openclaw mcp doctor gbrain --probe openclaw gateway start ``` `mcp add`, `login` and `doctor --probe` refuse while the local gateway runs, so stop it first and start it again after. `openclaw mcp login` runs the browser sign-in (on a headless host it prints a `--code` command to finish with). OpenClaw registers its client through dynamic client registration, so the brain owner turns that on and approves the consent ([native OAuth path](../guides/hosted-harness-access.md#native-oauth-path), [self-service registration](ADMIN.md#self-service-dynamic-registration)). Until the login succeeds, OpenClaw leaves the server out of agent turns. Publish the endpoint with `gbrain mcp expose` ([remote MCP](../guides/remote-mcp.md)). ### Or: a thin client's stdio bridge When OpenClaw should keep a stdio entry, install gbrain on the OpenClaw machine as a thin client of the brain host and register its `gbrain serve`, which relays every call to the host with that client's grant (it opens no local database). On the brain host, `gbrain agent register` with `--harness openclaw` prints these lines with your client filled in; run them on the OpenClaw machine: ```bash gbrain init --mcp-only --issuer-url https:// --mcp-url https:///mcp \ --oauth-client-id --oauth-client-secret openclaw mcp add gbrain --command "$(command -v gbrain)" --arg serve --arg --surface --arg starter --arg --advertise --arg verbs ``` If gbrain's bundle plugin is installed there, it already registers gbrain: run only the `init` line. To keep this client apart from another gbrain on that machine, put `GBRAIN_HOME=

` before the `init` line and add `--env GBRAIN_HOME=` to the `mcp add` line. What the bridge relays and how it reports failures: [stdio bridge](../architecture/thin-client.md#stdio-bridge). ## One bot for several people, in DMs When one OpenClaw bot answers several people, each in their own DM, each DM can read only the pages that person may read. The bot speaks to the brain as a [shared agent](../tutorials/company-brain.md#two-scoping-models-pick-the-one-that-matches-your-shape): every call carries an `X-Gbrain-On-Behalf-Of` header naming the person, and the brain answers with that person's view, within the bot's own source grant. On OpenClaw a small plugin sets the header from the DM's sender through the [requester-scoped MCP connection resolver](https://docs.openclaw.ai/plugins/sdk-overview/infrastructure) (`api.registerMcpServerConnectionResolver`). OpenClaw supplies the sender, not the model, and the header rides on the transport; an audience put in tool arguments is refused (`on_behalf_of_in_arguments`). **Say to your agent:** *"Set up my OpenClaw bot so each DM reads only what that person may read"*, then *"Show what alice-example's DMs can read"* (it runs `gbrain access check --token *** --as alice-example` on the brain host). **DMs only.** The resolver learns who sent the turn (`requesterSenderId`, with `messageChannel` and `agentAccountId`), not whether the turn came from a group or who else is in it. On a group turn the sender's view would be shown to the whole group. Use this recipe only on a gateway where every conversation has one person in it: set [`groupPolicy: "disabled"`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/groups) on each channel and turn `dm.groupEnabled` off on Discord and Slack. Group audiences are tracked in #8534. ### Before you share a personal brain through the bot Each DM reads as one member, so anything that relaxes privacy for a single member relaxes it for every person the bot serves: - **No private-pages grant on the bot.** Never give its token `--private-pages granted-sources`. With it, every mapped person reads every `visibility: private` page in the bot's sources, which on a personal brain are your own private pages. - **No private-facts grant on the bot.** Leave its token at `--private-facts none`. A DM call that names a person never uses that grant (an asserted audience reads world-only facts), so it adds nothing for the people the bot serves, and any call that reaches the brain without the header would read every fact saved private in the bot's sources. - **Host hatches off.** `GBRAIN_REMOTE_PRIVATE_PAGES` and `search.remote_private_pages` apply to every remote caller on the host, this bot included. Leave both unset while the bot runs. - **A dedicated token bound to no member.** Make a new token for the bot. Don't reuse your own agent's token or bind the bot's token to your member: your DMs through the bot then read like anyone else's, and your own agent keeps your full view. - **Pages only you should read name you as their reader.** Today `access: private` and `visibility: private` hide a page from this bot. Clearing those labels, by hand or in bulk with `gbrain repair private-labels`, makes the pages readable in every DM and by `guest`. Before you clear them, give the pages you want to keep to yourself `readable_by: []` or a folder rule (`gbrain access rule add --prefix / --readers `). `gbrain access check --token *** --as ` must show `Private pages: none` for the bot. ### Keep the gateway's people apart too The header separates the brain's answers. The rest of the gateway has to keep people apart as well ([OpenClaw's trust model](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security/trust-model) treats one gateway as one trust boundary, so people who must not trust each other need separate gateways): - [`session.dmScope: "per-channel-peer"`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/session) (`per-account-channel-peer` with several accounts on one channel). The default, `main`, puts every DM in one session, so one person's brain results land in the next person's context. - `tools.sessions.visibility: "self"`, so session tools can't read another person's DM transcript. - No shell or file tools for this agent on the gateway host: commands there inherit the gateway's environment, which holds the bot's token, and a local `gbrain` or database URL reads every page. - Leave the `gbrain-context-engine` slot unset for this bot. It reads through the host's own brain connection, not the bot's token. ### On the brain host Run `gbrain serve --http` ([deploy guide](DEPLOY.md)). Add each person as a member, make a read-only token for the bot, and list whom it may act for: each person's member id, plus `guest` for senders who have none. Never `*`. ```bash gbrain access member add alice-example gbrain access member add bob-example gbrain auth create openclaw-dm-bot --scopes read # prints the token once gbrain auth rescope --token *** --sources --may-act-for alice-example,bob-example,guest gbrain access check --token *** --as alice-example ``` **Keep the token read-only.** An audience limits which existing pages a write can reach, not where a new page lands. A write-capable token keeps its own write grant whatever the header says, so a page made in one DM outside a ruled folder (a new top-level page, a `capture` into `inbox/`) is read by everyone the source admits, `guest` included, unless the write names `readable_by`, which is the model's choice and not a fence. If the bot has to write for people who must not affect each other's data, register one client per person with `--bound-slug-prefixes /` ([Model B](../tutorials/company-brain.md#two-scoping-models-pick-the-one-that-matches-your-shape)); the resolver can return each sender's own credential. ### On the OpenClaw host Put the token in the gateway's environment as `GBRAIN_DM_BOT_TOKEN`, never in `openclaw.json`. Declare the server by URL alone. This replaces Option 2's stdio entry, and an `mcp.servers` entry also takes the place of the bundle plugin's server of the same name: ```bash openclaw mcp set gbrain '{"url":"https://brain.example.com/mcp","transport":"streamable-http"}' ``` Then write the plugin, a directory `gbrain-dm-audience` with three files. `package.json`: ```json { "name": "gbrain-dm-audience", "version": "1.0.0", "private": true, "type": "module", "openclaw": { "extensions": ["./index.js"] } } ``` `openclaw.plugin.json`: ```json { "id": "gbrain-dm-audience", "name": "GBrain DM audience", "description": "Names each DM's sender to gbrain as X-Gbrain-On-Behalf-Of", "configSchema": { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false, "properties": { "url": { "type": "string" }, "members": { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": { "type": "string" } } } } } ``` `index.js`: ```js export default { id: 'gbrain-dm-audience', name: 'GBrain DM audience', description: "Names each DM's sender to gbrain as X-Gbrain-On-Behalf-Of", register(api) { const { url, members = {} } = api.pluginConfig ?? {}; api.registerMcpServerConnectionResolver({ serverName: 'gbrain', resolve(ctx) { const token = process.env.GBRAIN_DM_BOT_TOKEN; if (!url || !token || !ctx.requesterSenderId) return null; const sender = `${ctx.messageChannel ?? ''}:${ctx.requesterSenderId}`; const audience = Object.hasOwn(members, sender) ? members[sender] : 'guest'; return { url, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ***}`, 'X-Gbrain-On-Behalf-Of': audience } }; }, }); }, }; ``` Install and enable it, map each sender to a member, and restart the gateway. A sender key is `:` as OpenClaw passes them. Map only ids the channel authenticates, such as numeric user ids, never display names or nicknames. ```bash openclaw plugins install --link ./gbrain-dm-audience --force --accept-capabilities openclaw plugins enable gbrain-dm-audience openclaw config set plugins.entries.gbrain-dm-audience.config '{"url":"https://brain.example.com/mcp","members":{"telegram:":"alice-example"}}' --strict-json ``` ### What each DM gets - A mapped sender reads as their member: the pages every member may read, plus pages whose `readable_by` or folder rule lists them, within the bot's sources. - An unmapped sender reads as `guest`: no restricted page and no private page. To give unmapped senders no brain at all, return `null` from `resolve` when `members` has no entry for the sender. - A mapped member outside `--may-act-for` is refused (`on_behalf_of_not_permitted`), and one that names no enabled member is refused (`on_behalf_of_unknown_member`); nothing is read either way ([shared-agent refusals](../guides/write-refusals.md#shared-agent-refusals)). - Runs without a trusted sender (cron, heartbeat, subagents) get no gbrain server from the resolver. Scheduled jobs that use the [wrapper below](#scheduled-jobs-and-workspace-scripts) read as the brain owner, so never send their output to someone's DM. To stop the bot reading for someone, take them out of `--may-act-for`. gbrain reads that list on every call; OpenClaw may keep a resolved connection for a few minutes. To check from a DM, ask the bot to call `whoami`: its `access.applied` names the audience the call read as, and `relaxation` must read `none`. ## Brain-first instructions Registering the server only makes the tools available. Agents seldom call a brain nobody told them about, so finish either option with the primary route, the per-turn rule: ```bash gbrain setup openclaw # --dry-run previews; --workspace picks the agent ``` It writes one short marked block into the workspace `AGENTS.md` (from `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` or `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`: a sole agent's workspace, else `agents.defaults.workspace`, else `~/.openclaw/workspace`; with several agents, pass `--workspace`). Text outside the markers is never touched, a re-run upgrades the block in place, `--no-instructions` opts out and is remembered, and `--remove` takes it out. A thin-client install puts the same block at the top of `GBRAIN-INSTRUCTIONS.md`. A rule in `AGENTS.md` reaches the system prompt only, so setup also puts it next to every user turn with a hook-only OpenClaw plugin, `gbrain-turn-rule`: its `before_prompt_build` handler returns the rule as `prependContext` (without its closing "answer" sentence on heartbeat, cron and exec-completion turns). The plugin is self-contained (the rule text is in its code; it reads and calls nothing) and lives in `/gbrain/gbrain-turn-rule`. Setup installs it with OpenClaw's own CLI: ```bash openclaw plugins install --link /gbrain/gbrain-turn-rule --force --accept-capabilities openclaw plugins enable gbrain-turn-rule openclaw config set plugins.entries.gbrain-turn-rule.hooks.allowConversationAccess true ``` OpenClaw requires `allowConversationAccess` before a non-bundled plugin's `before_prompt_build` runs. With no `openclaw` on PATH, setup writes the plugin and prints those commands to run on the OpenClaw host; restart a running gateway afterwards. `--no-instructions` and `--remove` uninstall the plugin and delete its directory. A re-run after an upgrade rewrites the plugin with the new text. Every agent on the gateway gets the plugin's rule, so a `--workspace` run leaves it when it would name another server and `--no-instructions` there keeps it. OpenClaw lists no gbrain tool after `openclaw mcp set`: the model reaches them only through `tool_search`, whose results it frames as external data. With an MCP connection the rule therefore names the tools (`recall`, `entity`, `search`, `query`) and says to find them with `tool_search` and run them with `tool_call`. With `openclaw` on PATH, setup runs `openclaw plugins inspect gbrain-turn-rule --runtime --json` and exits non-zero with `turn_hook_not_loaded` unless the plugin shows as loaded with `before_prompt_build` ([repair](../guides/repair.md#turn-hook-not-loaded)). ## Skills (fallback) `gbrain skillpack scaffold --harness openclaw` adds gbrain's skills to the workspace. OpenClaw lists them in its prompt, but in harness-evals a listed skill was followed on 1-3% of turns against 97-100% for the per-turn rule, so install skills beside the rule, never instead of it. OpenClaw serves a skill only whole: a SKILL.md larger than one read (64,000 characters on a model with 200k+ context, 32,000 at 100k-200k, 16,000 below, a 32,768-byte page when the context window is unknown) gets "cannot be partially served" and nothing else. Every SKILL.md gbrain installs for OpenClaw is at most 32,000 bytes (`test/openclaw-route.test.ts`), so it loads on any model with 100k+ context and when the window is unknown; on smaller models the 16,000-character cap applies and the larger skills do not load. ## Scheduled jobs and workspace scripts OpenClaw cron jobs, workspace scripts and hooks run with another `HOME` and environment than the gateway's MCP server. Route every one of them through a single wrapper that sets `GBRAIN_HOME`, loads the brain's env file and runs the installed `gbrain` by absolute path; log its stderr and check its exit code ([the wrapper and its rules](../guides/cron-schedule.md#calling-gbrain-unattended)). On a managed brain, scripts commit the files they write with `gbrain git commit-push -- ` (never plain `git commit`); a scheduled `gbrain sources refresh ` keeps it current ([scripts and the managed checkout](../guides/shared-checkout-git.md#scripts-and-the-managed-checkout)). ## Have gbrain report back to this chat When the brain owner has turned on [reporting back](../guides/wakeshift.md) (`gbrain wakeshift enable` on the brain host), gbrain can wake an OpenClaw session when a job, a pending write or a cron run it watches finishes. OpenClaw needs Wakeshift's own plugin for that. Where the gateway runs (in its container, if it's in one): ```bash gbrain setup openclaw --wakeshift ``` It asks for consent, then runs OpenClaw's installer for the pinned `@wakeshift/openclaw@1.4.31` (`openclaw plugins install npm:@wakeshift/openclaw@1.4.31 --force --accept-capabilities`, then `openclaw plugins enable wakeshift --accept-capabilities`) and checks that the plugin loads. The plugin turns on OpenClaw's hooks endpoint with its own token. On a gateway that listens beyond this computer, setup prints Wakeshift's question about that endpoint; agreeing is yours to do (`openclaw config set plugins.entries.wakeshift.config.allowNetworkHooks true --strict-json`), and gbrain never sets it. The session shows a note starting `Wakeshift: connected` after its first watch. `gbrain doctor` warns when the installed plugin is not the pinned version. Remove it with `openclaw wakeshift reset && openclaw plugins uninstall wakeshift --force`. ## Verify `openclaw mcp list` should show `gbrain`. Then start an agent turn and ask it to use the brain: ``` Call get_brain_identity, then search my brain for [topic]. ``` If the tools respond, the wiring works. `list_skills` shows everything the brain can do (gated by `mcp.publish_skills` on the host). ## Remove Delete `mcp.servers.gbrain` from `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` (or run `openclaw mcp remove gbrain` if your version has it), or uninstall the bundle plugin. # AGENT_OPERATOR v1: how an agent operates gbrain gbrain assumes an AI agent is its operator. Every failure, refusal, degraded result and recommendation gbrain produces (MCP tool results, CLI human output, CLI `--json`, doctor, readiness) carries the same machine contract: a stable `code`, a reason, one next step with who acts and whether the user must agree first, and a read-only way to verify it worked. This page is that contract, `contract_version: 1`. Related pages: [error codes](../guides/error-codes.md) (one row per `code`; offline: `gbrain errors `), [exit codes](../guides/exit-codes.md), [`_meta` channels](MCP_META_CHANNELS.md), [memory verbs](MEMORY_VERBS_v1.md). ## Quick contract 1. Read `code` (fall back to `error` on older servers). `message` says what happened, `why` says why. 2. Follow `fix.next`: - `run` → run `fix.argv` (CLI) or call `fix.mcp` (MCP) exactly as given. - `ask_user` → relay `user_message` to the user and stop; run the fix only after they agree. - `tell_user_to_run` → give the user `fix.command`; it needs them or the brain host's operator. - `wait` → retry after the stated delay with the same request. - `report` → tell the user what happened and run `gbrain doctor --json`. 3. Then run `fix.verify` (always read-only) to confirm the fix worked. 4. Treat `[gbrain notice …]` blocks and `[AGENT]` blocks the same way. A degraded result is not proof of "no notes": a result stamped `[gbrain degraded: …]` (`_meta.degraded`, the CLI `degraded` key) is partial. ## Transcripts These are generated from the frozen wire goldens in `test/fixtures/agent-contract/v1/` by `bun run build:agent-protocol`; the goldens never store `next`, so the generator recomputes it with the same decision table gbrain uses at render time. Docs URLs on the wire are pinned to the installed version; the transcripts show `master`. Transcripts marked "journey" are recorded from real CLI and stdio MCP runs by the deterministic agent journey (`test/agent-journey.serial.test.ts`); machine values (home directory, pids, ids, times) show as fixed examples. ### 1. A caller mistake over MCP: `run` A harness on stdio MCP (surface `full`) lists pages with a sort key that does not exist. ```text list_pages {"sort":"bogus"} ``` gbrain returns (`isError: true`, the envelope shown parsed): ```json { "error": "invalid_params", "code": "invalid_params", "message": "Unknown sort 'bogus'.", "suggestion": "Use one of: updated, created, title. Next: list_pages {\"sort\":\"updated\"}", "docs": "https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/blob/master/docs/guides/error-codes.md#invalid_params", "fix": { "argv": [ "gbrain", "list", "--sort", "updated", "--brain", "host", "--source", "default" ], "command": "gbrain list --sort updated --brain host --source default", "mcp": { "tool": "list_pages", "arguments": { "sort": "updated" } }, "consent": [], "actor": "agent", "next": "run", "why": "updated is the default sort.", "verify": { "mcp": { "tool": "list_pages", "arguments": { "sort": "updated", "limit": 1 } } }, "requires_exclusive": false }, "docs_cmd": [ "gbrain", "errors", "invalid_params" ], "class": "caller", "retryable": false, "contract_version": 1 } ``` The result is one content block. The agent reads `code: invalid_params` and `fix.next: run`, so it calls `list_pages {"sort":"updated"}` itself, then confirms with the read-only `list_pages {"sort":"updated","limit":1}`. Nothing needs the user. ### 2. Paid work without approval on the CLI: `ask_user`, exit 3 An agent runs remediation from a non-interactive shell without `--yes` or `--max-usd`. ```bash gbrain doctor --remediate --json ``` stdout (`--json`): ```json { "status": "confirmation_required", "error": "confirmation_required", "code": "confirmation_required", "message": "doctor --remediate needs the user's approval before it runs; nothing was changed.", "suggestion": "Ask the user: Fixing your brain's health will cost about $0.40 in embedding calls. OK to proceed? If they agree, run: gbrain doctor --remediate --max-usd 0.60 --yes --brain host", "effects": [ "paid" ], "actor": "agent", "why": "Remediation re-embeds 120 stale pages through the configured provider.", "risk": "Spends up to the cap on embedding calls; no data is deleted.", "est_usd": 0.4, "user_message": "Fixing your brain's health will cost about $0.40 in embedding calls. OK to proceed?", "fix": { "argv": [ "gbrain", "doctor", "--remediate", "--max-usd", "0.60", "--yes", "--brain", "host" ], "command": "gbrain doctor --remediate --max-usd 0.60 --yes --brain host", "consent": [ "paid" ], "actor": "agent", "next": "ask_user", "why": "Remediation re-embeds 120 stale pages through the configured provider.", "user_message": "Fixing your brain's health will cost about $0.40 in embedding calls. OK to proceed?", "requires_exclusive": false, "preview_argv": [ "gbrain", "doctor", "--remediation-plan", "--json", "--brain", "host" ] }, "preview": { "argv": [ "gbrain", "doctor", "--remediation-plan", "--json", "--brain", "host" ], "command": "gbrain doctor --remediation-plan --json --brain host" }, "preapprove_argv": [ "gbrain", "config", "set", "consent.preapprove.paid.max_usd_per_run", "" ], "docs_cmd": [ "gbrain", "errors", "confirmation_required" ], "contract_version": 1 } ``` Without `--json`, the same refusal prints as an `[AGENT]` block: ```text [AGENT] ask: Fixing your brain's health will cost about $0.40 in embedding calls. OK to proceed? why: Remediation re-embeds 120 stale pages through the configured provider. risk: Spends up to the cap on embedding calls; no data is deleted. consent: paid actor: agent next: ask_user if_yes: gbrain doctor --remediate --max-usd 0.60 --yes --brain host — To stop asking for runs under a limit the user picks: gbrain config set consent.preapprove.paid.max_usd_per_run '' if_no: Nothing runs; nothing was changed. To look first (read-only): gbrain doctor --remediation-plan --json --brain host [SHOW USER] Fixing your brain's health will cost about $0.40 in embedding calls. OK to proceed? [/SHOW USER] [/AGENT] ``` Nothing ran and the command exited 3. The agent reads `fix.next: ask_user`, relays `user_message` ("Fixing your brain's health will cost about $0.40 in embedding calls. OK to proceed?") and stops. It may offer the read-only preview `gbrain doctor --remediation-plan --json --brain host`. Only after the user agrees does it run `gbrain doctor --remediate --max-usd 0.60 --yes --brain host`. Passing `--yes` on its own would be a consent violation even though gbrain cannot tell the difference. ### 3. An empty recall with a notice: `tell_user_to_run` A harness on stdio MCP searches a keyless brain and nothing matches. ```text search {"query":"…"} ``` gbrain returns these content blocks: `content[0]`: ```json [] ``` `content[1]`: ```text [gbrain notice empty_retrieval kind=info] why: No pages matched. Search ran keyword-only because embeddings are not configured. fix: gbrain doctor --json --brain host next: tell_user_to_run user_message: I found no notes on that topic. Your brain searches keywords only right now. ``` ⚠️ [... middle content omitted — showing head and tail ...] in that reply: the settings in effect, the cost matrix and how to change each. Don't end the install on a question. Apply an answer with the option's `argv` whenever the user gives one. Nothing paid turns on from these settings without a key the user supplied. The steps: 1. Register gbrain with the harness using the `harness_wiring` fix. The registration always uses the absolute gbrain path and `--surface starter`, started through gbrain's launcher (for example `gbrain setup claude-code --no-hooks --gbrain-bin /abs/path/gbrain`, which registers `/hook-launcher/gbrain-hook /abs/path/gbrain serve --surface starter`; `gbrain init --surface ` changes the surface it prints). 2. Run `gbrain doctor --only harness_wiring --json`, a read-only smoke check: it reads the registration, then either finds the registered server already running or starts it and runs initialize, tools/list and one `recall`. 3. `remember` an install-check marker with provenance `install-check`, ask the user to restart the harness, `recall` it in the new session, then `forget` it. Never save a made-up fact about the user. ## Make gbrain work better for your user When gbrain sees the setup limiting what the user is trying to do, it says so with a `coaching` notice or a doctor or readiness row. You can also check proactively: `gbrain doctor --json` lists readiness for embeddings, chat LLM, worker, writeback, backup, tool surface, sync, migrations and harness wiring, each with a `fix`. - **Wire the harness.** A harness without gbrain registered cannot recall or remember. Use the `harness_wiring` fix; when several sessions or harnesses share one brain, they share one `gbrain serve --http` instead of competing stdio servers. - **Writeback.** With ambient writeback off, the brain only learns what the user explicitly asks you to remember. Ask before turning it on (`gbrain config set memory.auto_writeback salient`). - **Search quality.** A keyless brain searches keywords only. Enabling embeddings needs a provider key and costs money (`credentials`, `paid`): ask first, then use the exact command the readiness fix names. It keeps pages and facts. - **Maintenance.** An open `gbrain serve` runs free upkeep while idle (`gbrain maintain --status`). Without a worker, queued jobs wait. `gbrain maintain --schedule` and `gbrain autopilot --install` install a background service (`persistent_install`): ask first. - **Backup.** Repo backups exclude database-only pages and facts. When the `backup_coverage` notice fires, tell the user what is unprotected. - **Surface.** `--surface verbs` (memory verbs), `starter` or `full` decides which tools you see; every stdio registration gbrain writes pins `starter`. When you call a real tool outside the session's surface, the `unknown_tool` fix is `request_tools {"surface":"full"}` (`next: run`): it widens this session only, sends `tools/list_changed` and returns the new tools' schemas, so call them by name. Where `request_tools` is not callable (the `verbs` surface, `--access read-only`, or `mcp.allow_session_widen` off), the fix is the CLI equivalent rendered `tell_user_to_run`, and its `why` names the lasting route: `GBRAIN_SURFACE=full` in the env of the harness's MCP server entry for gbrain. Coach at most once per topic, at a natural point, and never about something the user turned off on purpose. ## Conformance fixtures for harness authors `test/fixtures/agent-contract/v1/` holds the frozen wire shapes: object result, bare-array result with a notice, error with fix, error with notices, nested legacy error, receipt-bearing error, legacy `error` value with new `code`, the `confirmation_required` payload, the notice block text and the `--json` fallback document.
